dataset_family: BioFIND (MRC CBU Cambridge + CTB Madrid; 117 MCI with follow-up: 64 AD progression / 53 stable; 104 with MRI)
method_family: Two-layer stacking: first-layer ridge classifiers per modality (Riemannian tangent-space MEG covariance and power-envelope, vectorised dwPLI, 64 FreeSurfer volumes) plus scalar site/age/sex/education/MMSE inputs, with a regularised logistic-regression second layer, 10x10-fold CV. Also nested non-regularised logistic regression models (in-sample AUC, bootstrap CIs).
same_sample_or_cohort_as: P-577 (registry duplicate of this paper; must not be counted separately)
P-173 (Madrid MEG cohort; possible overlap with BioFIND's CTB Madrid participants, not verified)
what_it_shows: In cross-validated stacking, combining all inputs gave AUC 0.81 (SD 0.12). This beat MRI cortical volumes alone (0.77, SD 0.14), MEG covariance alone (0.74, SD 0.13) and every single clinical or demographic variable (MMSE about 0.68 and site about 0.64 in Fig. 5a medians). Conditional permutation importance shows the full model relied on MEG covariance, MMSE, MRI and site. In the in-sample logistic models, adding MEG beta power to age+education+MMSE+hippocampal ratio (Model 2, AUC 0.75, to Model 4, 0.84) gave a bootstrap CI for the AUC difference of 0.026 to 0.179.
why: PDF identity: the title, authors (Gaubert, Garces, Hipp, Bruna, Lopez, Maestu, Vaghari, Henson, Paquet, Engemann), eBioMedicine 2025 114:105659 and the DOI match the P-488 block; P-577 is its registry duplicate. The study runs a within-study head-to-head of a fused model against unimodal models, outside ADNI. Stated form, 'partly': the full stacked model beats each unimodal brain model and each single clinical variable. However, (1) the gain over the best unimodal model (MRI 0.77 to full 0.81) lies within the fold SDs, and no formal test of full vs best marginal is reported for the CV model. The discussion's 'significantly enhanced' (p.17) is not backed by a reported test; Fig. 5a shows non-overlapping 95% CIs of the median over 100 CV splits, but CV splits are not independent. (2) The full model includes site, which the authors state is collinear with progression: 23/27 CBU participants progressed vs 41/90 at CTB. Site is a significant CPI contributor (p = 0.046), so part of the fused model's advantage rests on a non-transportable site proxy. (3) What fusion adds is mainly a second primary brain modality (resting MEG, three metrics) plus MMSE and demographics. This is generic multimodal stacking, not auxiliary-data-aware fusion as the ledger defines it (metadata, source-task attention, side-information). Narrowed form, 'partly': the full model does add auxiliary information (MMSE, age, sex, education, site) to the MRI model and improves on MRI alone (0.77 to 0.81). But the auxiliary contribution is never isolated from the MEG contribution, because no MRI+clinical stacked model is reported. The one clearly significant logistic comparison (Model 2 to Model 4) adds MEG, a brain modality, to a model that already holds the clinical variables. It is in-sample, and there is no MRI-only logistic model. The authors themselves flag circularity in how the MEG power feature was chosen (p.9). Other caveats: internal CV only, no external test; follow-up durations are not documented per patient (about 3 years at Cambridge, 5 at Madrid); and the AD diagnosis is clinical, without CSF or PET. Independence: BioFIND is a non-ADNI dataset family, which would be new for VF-15. The Madrid (CTB) portion may overlap the Madrid MEG cohort of P-173; I did not verify this, and P-173 is neither a supporter nor my candidate. The method family (stacked regularised linear models on Riemannian MEG + MRI) differs from P-3, P-104 and P-81. No shared authors with the supporters (Luo et al.; Shen, Zhu et al.; Cao, Ma, Nayak, Duong). Peer-reviewed journal article, not a preprint. Fig. 5a values were read from a PyMuPDF render of p.15 saved at out/VF-15/img/P-488_p15.png.

quotes.quote: The best marginal performance was observed for MEG covariances (AUC = 0.74, SD = 0.13) and MRI cortical volumes (AUC = 0.77, SD = 0.14). Combining all inputs led to markedly improved classification scores (AUC = 0.81, SD = 0.12), suggesting synergies between the different modalities.
Analysis of conditional permutation importance (CPI)93,94—accounting for shared information between variables—revealed that the full model relied on MEG covariances, MMSE, MRI and site (Fig. 5b).

The results suggest that the performance of the full model was based on statistically complementary information from the MEG covariance, MMSE and MRI but also highlighted potential contributions from site effects.

AD-progressors were overrepresented in the CBU site as compared to the CTB site. ... the unequal distribution of progression cases across sites has as a consequence that direct controlling for site-effects may reduce the signal-to-noise for statistical analysis modelling of progression risk as site is, to a certain extent, collinear with progression risk.
Model 2 combining age, education, MMSE and hippocampus/total grey matter ratio had a 0.75 AUC (95% CI: 0.67–0.85), a sensitivity of 72% and a specificity of 72%.

Model 4 combining age, education, MMSE, cluster MEG power and Hippocampus/Total grey matter ratio achieved slightly better results than Model 3 with an AUC of 0.84 (95% CI: 0.78–0.92), a sensitivity of 80% and a specificity of 74%.

In contrast, the comparison between Model 2 and Model 4 showed a much clearer, significant difference, with a confidence interval from 0.026 to 0.179, highlighting a substantial improvement in Model 4’s discrimination capacity over Model 2 that only used MRI.
It also increased the risk of circularity as our choice of the MEG power was based on visual-statistical exploration.

recruited from two sites: 68 patients from the MRC Cognition & Brain Sciences Unit (CBU) at the University of Cambridge and 90 patients from the Laboratory of Cognitive and Computational Neuroscience at the Centre for Biomedical Technology (CTB), Madrid.
